overview: Sanford is New Zealand's largest integrated seafood company, listed on the NZX (fiscal year ends 30 September, so 'FY25' means the year to 30 September 2025 and 'HY26' the six months to 31 March 2026). It operates across three pillars: Wildcatch (deepwater and inshore quota fishing of scampi, hoki, squid, orange roughy and Antarctic toothfish, processed largely through its Timaru factory), Aquaculture Salmon (King Salmon farmed in Big Glory Bay, Stewart Island, processed at Bluff) and Greenshell Mussels (farmed in Marlborough and the Coromandel, processed at Havelock). The company owns one of New Zealand's largest books of fishing quota (Individual Transferable Quota under the Quota Management System, ~19.8% of the country's total quota) and marine farm licences, sells predominantly into export markets (North America, Europe, China, Australia), and is currently mid-way through a 'Back to Basics' operational turnaround under Managing Director David Mair (appointed May 2024).

business_model.summary: Sanford converts owned/leased fishing quota (Annual Catch Entitlement, ACE, derived from owned quota under the QMS) and owned marine farm water space into processed seafood sold mostly into export markets. Wildcatch is a mature, quota-capped commodity business (deepwater trawling/longlining plus ACE leasing to Moana New Zealand for inshore species); Aquaculture (Salmon and Mussels) is the growth and margin engine, contributing the bulk of segment EBIT despite being a minority of revenue ($106.1m of HY26's $270.2m revenue but $47.3m of the period's EBIT). Revenue is transactional/commodity-priced (no long-term offtake contracts disclosed) but volumes are underpinned by durable quota and consented farm space, so the asset base is closer to annuity-like even though realised pricing is highly cyclical. A smaller, higher-margin value-add stream (Greenshell mussel oil / nutraceutical and premium branded product) rides on top of bulk commodity mussel and salmon sales, supporting the mix-driven margin gains management has reported.

revenue_streams.name: Other Wildcatch species (squid, toothfish, orange roughy, ling, inshore ACE leasing)

business_model.customer_type: B2B export-focused; wholesale/distributor and food-service customers in North America, Europe, China, Australia and NZ domestic food service; no single customer over 10% of HY26 sales (one customer exceeded 10% in FY25 and H1-FY25)
business_model.geographic_mix: FY25 sales by region: North America 27%, Europe 21%, New Zealand 18%, China 15%, Australia 7%, Other 12%. HY26 revenue by delivery destination: NZ 35%, North America 16%, Europe 15%, China 13%, Australia 9%, other Asia/rest 12%

main_competitors: Talley's Group (private, NZ's largest privately-owned seafood company)
Moana New Zealand / Aotearoa Fisheries Limited (iwi-owned, Sanford's inshore ACE lessee)
New Zealand King Salmon (NZK.NZ, Marlborough Sounds salmon farmer)
international salmon and mussel farmers (Chile, Norway, Australia)
competitive_position.market_position: New Zealand's largest listed integrated seafood company by revenue and quota holding (~19.8% of national QMS quota, allocating 75,000+ green-weight tonnes of ACE across 300+ fish stocks in FY25); one of only two significant NZ king salmon farmers; dominant Greenshell mussel processor via Havelock and Coromandel/WMOL arrangements

moat_factors.description: Sanford holds ~19.8% of New Zealand's total QMS quota across 300+ individual fish stocks, generating 75,000+ tonnes of Annual Catch Entitlement in FY25, carried as roughly $486m of intangible assets (about 48% of total assets and 66% of shareholder equity at FY25/HY26). New entrants cannot create quota; it is a fixed, perpetual right that can only be acquired from existing holders (or occasionally reallocated by the Crown), creating a structural supply barrier that underpins the company's long-term asset value irrespective of any single year's catch price.

Big Glory Bay salmon consents and Marlborough/Coromandel mussel farm consents are scarce and slow to obtain; the Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024 extended Sanford's coastal mussel permits to 2044, materially de-risking the mussel asset base and supporting further investment.

Owned processing (Bluff for salmon, Havelock for mussels, Timaru for wildcatch) and fleet gives cost and quality control, but the fleet is aging and capital-hungry to maintain (five-year dry-dock recertification cycles, some vessels 30+ years old).

moat_factors.factor: Scale in a small domestic industry
moat_factors.description: Largest listed NZ seafood company gives some purchasing, freight and market-access scale versus smaller operators, though Talley's (private) is comparable or larger in some categories.

weaknesses: Salmon production is hard-capped at Big Glory Bay by a nitrogen/environmental discharge limit — management states the company is close to its maximum harvest with 'no growth expectations in FY26 beyond what can be produced at Big Glory Bay', so the highest-margin segment cannot simply scale with demand without new (higher-risk, higher-capital) sites
Wildcatch is explicitly described by management as 'operating as a commodity player' with catch volumes capped by the QMS and limited growth optionality

No long-term contracted pricing disclosed — realised prices for scampi, hoki, salmon and mussels are set by global commodity/market dynamics and have been volatile (e.g., scampi price roughly halved off its highs; squid pricing swung sharply within a single fiscal year)
Aging fleet requiring ongoing capital renewal (five-year dry-dock surveys, new vessels being built to replace much older boats)

Complex, historically confused organisational structure — the new MD explicitly flagged that a prior attempt to create business-unit divisions had never been properly implemented and caused decision-making bureaucracy, which is only now being fixed

Book value materially understates true asset value: quota intangibles are carried at historic cost under NZ IFRS, not fair/market value, so the balance sheet (and any P/B-style comparison) is a conservative floor rather than a fair reflection of the quota's replacement or market value — a genuine business strength, but one that makes headline P/B multiples look more expensive than the underlying asset backing actually is

growth_drivers: Continued SKU rationalisation and pricing/margin discipline in Sales & Marketing, credited for 'sustainable business improvements' in gross margin rather than one-off gains

Mussel volume growth at low capital risk: new consent granted for mussel farming water space in the Western Firth of Thames (first harvest ~March 2027), a new purpose-built 30m aluminium farming vessel, record SPATnz hatchery spat production, and the 20-year RMA permit extension to 2044 enabling further investment
Processing productivity and yield improvements (Havelock mussel factory yield gains were a primary driver of the FY25 mussel profit surge)
Shift from a 'push' farming/production model to a demand-driven 'pull' model across salmon and (next) mussels, intended to reduce waste and better match supply to customer demand

Market diversification away from China/US concentration — management is actively rebuilding relationships in Japan (with Maruha Nichiro Corporation, a top shareholder at ~4.7%), South Korea and Southeast Asia

Balance sheet repair (net debt cut from $185.5m at FY24-end to $93.4m at FY25-end and to $102.1m at HY26, interest cost down from $16.9m to $12.1m) freeing capacity for future growth investment once the strategic review of wildcatch/aquaculture assets concludes
Potential for open-ocean or expanded aquaculture consenting longer-term, though management explicitly frames this as 'High Capital – High Risk' and not yet committed to
Secular tailwind of rising global protein demand supporting seafood pricing generally

Unused Sanford water space where infrastructure already exists but is not currently being actively farmed — management is assessing reactivating this footprint at relatively low incremental capital cost

business.risk: Salmon growth ceiling at Big Glory Bay
business.description: Harvest volume is capped by a nitrogen discharge/environmental limit, not by demand; FY26 guidance explicitly states no growth beyond current site capacity, so the best-margin segment cannot scale without a new, materially riskier site

business.risk: Commodity price volatility across all three pillars
business.description: Scampi (FY25 sales revenue down materially on price alone), mussels, hoki and squid prices swing sharply with global supply/demand and are not contracted long-term; FY25's record result was explicitly pricing-driven and management flags 'ongoing global turbulence' and the 'emergence of trading blocks'

A substantial cut to the East/South Chatham Rise orange roughy TACC (ORH 3B cut from 4,752 to 2,321 tonnes for the 2025-26 fishing year, with the East and South Chatham Rise sub-area limit reduced further to 324 tonnes and a proposed spawning-area closure from 1 June 2026 to allow stock rebuild) will constrain raw material supply and Timaru processing volumes; management says the lower Annual Catch Entitlement 'will have an impact on the whole New Zealand fishing industry and especially on our processing at Timaru'
One customer exceeded 10% of sales in FY25; North America and China together were ~42% of FY25 sales, exposing Sanford to bilateral trade-policy shocks in either market
Multiple vessels 30+ years old requiring dry-dock recertification (lost fishing days in FY25) and eventual costly replacement

business.risk: Execution risk of the 'Back to Basics' turnaround
business.description: MD (over two years into the role by HY26) is simultaneously overhauling org structure, supply-chain philosophy (push-to-pull), and conducting an unfinished strategic review of wildcatch and aquaculture assets — meaningful change management risk, and the 'no growth expectations' language suggests the easy wins are being harvested first while structural decisions remain pending

financial.description: Majority of revenue is export-denominated (USD, EUR, etc.) against an NZD cost base and reporting currency; the company uses forward FX contracts and derivative fair-value positions have swung between favourable and unfavourable across recent halves (hedge mark-to-market volatility flows through OCI/equity)

financial.risk: Interest rate exposure on floating debt
financial.description: Net debt of $102.1m at HY26 (down sharply from $185.5m at FY24-end); the Group uses interest rate swaps to fix 25-75% of floating exposure per Treasury Policy, and refinanced its bank facilities on 31 March 2026, reducing total facility limits from $160m to $140m
Chair/MD explicitly flag fuel, feed (salmon), electricity and labour cost inflation running ahead of pricing recovery ('we face a likely increase in costs faster than we will recover in pricing')

regulatory.risk: Quota Management System / TACC policy risk
regulatory.description: Total Allowable Catch and TACC decisions are set by the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries and can move against Sanford (as with the ORH 3B orange roughy cut and proposed spawning-area closures) as well as in its favour (SNA8 snapper, hoki and other TACC increases elsewhere); a March 2025 High Court ruling found ministerial changes to fishing quota 'capricious' in one case, underlining that TACC-setting carries genuine legal/process risk. This is a two-sided but ever-present risk to the core intangible asset base

Legislation introduced to Parliament in 2026 proposes modernising the Fisheries Act, adding flexibility to deemed-value rates for QMS stocks and easing barriers to industry growth; framed by government as pro-industry, but any material change to how catch limits are set or quota is valued is a structural risk (and possible opportunity) to the quota intangible given it represents roughly half of Sanford's balance sheet — environmental groups (e.g., Environmental Defence Society) have submitted opposing aspects of the bill, adding political uncertainty to its final form

Big Glory Bay's nitrogen cap and the general difficulty of obtaining new marine farm consents in New Zealand limit growth optionality; RMA changes have so far been favourable (20-year permit extension to 2044) but future consenting for new/expanded sites is not guaranteed

regulatory.risk: Cameras on boats / at-sea monitoring compliance
regulatory.description: New Zealand's phased rollout of on-board cameras for the commercial fishing fleet (electronic monitoring) increases compliance costs and scrutiny of bycatch/discards across Sanford's deepwater and inshore-linked fleet, with reputational risk if breaches are recorded

regulatory.risk: Marine protected areas / Hauraki Gulf restrictions
regulatory.description: Expanding marine protection (e.g., Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act changes restricting bottom trawling and dredging in parts of the Gulf) progressively removes fishing area from parts of the inshore fleet Sanford's ACE-leasing arrangements depend on, a slow-moving but structural headwind to wildcatch

Climate Reporting Disclosure (CRD) regime compliance threshold is expected to rise, likely exempting Sanford at its current market cap, but the company has voluntarily committed to continue CRD-equivalent disclosure

macro.description: US tariff escalation through FY25/FY26 has directly softened half-shell mussel demand/pricing and disrupted scampi and other trade flows into the US; management calls out 'ongoing global turbulence in markets and the emergence of trading blocks' as an ongoing risk to medium-term demand and pricing

Softening Chinese scampi demand has been attributed to restrained discretionary expenditure in a subdued Chinese economy; China remains a 'key market' management says it must maintain but the relationship carries macro cyclicality

Warming sea temperatures have caused severe mortality events at other NZ salmon farms — most notably NZ King Salmon's Marlborough Sounds/Pelorus Sound farms, which lost a large share of stock in a 2022 marine heatwave and have had to fallow farms. Sanford's Big Glory Bay site (Stewart Island) is geographically cooler and has historically been protected (disease-free, cold-water), which is a genuine locational advantage, but it is not immune to long-term ocean warming trends, and its hard nitrogen-cap ceiling means Sanford cannot simply relocate/expand capacity to a cooler alternative site without a costly new consenting process

macro.risk: Algal blooms and mussel spat availability
macro.description: Mussel farming remains exposed to biotoxin/algal bloom events and reliance on wild-caught spat from Kaitaia (partially mitigated by the SPATnz hatchery, which produced record spat volumes in FY25 and is being benchmarked directly against wild spat in the new Western Firth of Thames development)

macro.risk: Fuel cost / ETS pass-through on the deepwater fleet
macro.description: Diesel/marine fuel is a major direct cost for the deepwater and inshore fleet; New Zealand's Emissions Trading Scheme progressively raises the effective carbon cost embedded in fuel prices, and management has flagged fuel inflation running ahead of pricing recovery in some periods

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global seafood/protein demand is a structural grower, but New Zealand wildcatch volumes are fixed/declining under the QMS while aquaculture (salmon, mussels) is the industry's genuine growth vector, constrained by consenting and environmental limits rather than demand
macro_factors.cyclicality: High price cyclicality within a structurally stable volume base — realised prices for scampi, squid, hoki, salmon and mussels swing materially year to year with global supply/demand and trade policy, even though the underlying quota/consented water space is durable
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — capital-intensive vessel and farm infrastructure funded partly by bank debt; net debt materially reduced through FY25/HY26 has lowered sensitivity, and 25-75% of floating exposure is swapped to fixed
key_input_costs: Salmon feed (largest single cost in the salmon business, commodity-priced and volatile)

recent_developments.event: HY26 (six months to 31 March 2026) delivered record half-year adjusted EBIT ($65.0m, +20%), EBIT ($64.0m) and NPAT ($42.4m, +25%) despite sales revenue falling ~5.5% to $270.2m, driven by gross margin expansion to 33.7% (from 28.2%) on pricing, cost discipline and a $17.5m favourable salmon biological-asset fair-value gain (vs $3.3m in HY25); operating cash flow fell sharply to $13.7m (from $49.6m) due to increased frozen half-shell mussel inventory

Major shareholder Ngai Tahu Investments Limited sold approximately 8.97m shares (~9.6% of Sanford, roughly half its prior stake) via an underwritten overnight block trade at not less than $7.15/share, raising ~NZ$64m and reducing Ngai Tahu's holding to just under 20% (19.87%); the trade size was reported at roughly 1.3x the entire prior 12 months' trading volume, triggering a trading halt and weighing on the share price in the following weeks despite the strong HY26 result

Fisheries Amendment Bill 2026 introduced to Parliament, proposing to modernise the Fisheries Act and QMS deemed-value flexibility; Environmental Defence Society and other groups have made submissions opposing aspects of the bill
Bank refinancing completed 31 March 2026: total facility limit reduced from $160m to $140m, reflecting the lower debt requirement after aggressive FY25/HY26 debt paydown

Tony Carter (former Foodstuffs CEO and Air NZ Chair) appointed as an independent director, adding food/distribution-channel governance experience; Chair Sir Robert McLeod (in his 11th year on the Board) has announced his intention to retire from the Board during 2026
Annual Shareholders' Meeting held 17 December 2025 at Eden Park, Auckland, presenting the FY25 record result to shareholders

FY2025 'Back to Basics' record result: revenue roughly flat at $584.1m (FY24: $582.9m), gross margin up to 26.5% (from 21.6%), adjusted EBIT a record $105.2m (from $74.2m), NPAT more than tripled to $63.7m (from $19.7m), operating cash flow $135.3m (from $73.0m), net debt cut by $92.1m to $93.4m, EPS 68.1 cps (from 21.1 cps); final dividend held at 5.0 cps; Sanford named a finalist for the Deloitte Top 200 / BusinessNZ Most Improved Performance Award

Resource Management (Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms) Amendment Act 2024 allowed Sanford to extend its coastal mussel farm permits to 2044, materially de-risking the mussel asset base

Exit from direct North Island inshore fishing operations to an ACE-leasing model, with inshore quota now leased to Moana New Zealand (Aotearoa Fisheries Limited) rather than fished directly; Commerce Commission cleared aspects of the transaction; the NIML (Tauranga mussel processing) joint operation was closed and its assets sold in FY24/H1-FY25

David Mair (previously an independent director since November 2022, ex-Managing Director of Skellerup and former a2 Milk director) appointed Managing Director, launching the ongoing organisational, supply-chain ('push to pull') and strategic-review overhaul now branded 'Back to Basics'

guidance.as_of: HY2026 result and FY2025 Annual Report (David Mair, Managing Director)

items.vs_prior: maintained (structural ceiling, not a new constraint)
items.notes: Management explicit: 'There are no growth expectations in FY26 beyond what can be produced at Big Glory Bay' due to nitrogen cap constraints; focus is on productivity/yield from the Bluff processing facility instead of volume

items.notes: Feed is salmon's largest cost line and is commodity-priced, so management flags it can move quickly and dramatically despite the near-term steady outlook

items.vs_prior: lowered vs FY25's realised (unusually high) yields
items.notes: FY25 Havelock yields were unusually favourable due to climatic conditions; HY26 showed demand and price challenges leading to increased frozen half-shell inventory, and the second Coromandel/WMOL processing season is still working through teething issues

items.target: Prices expected to increase further given the TACC cut
items.notes: Driven by the East Chatham Rise ORH 3B TACC cut and proposed spawning-area closure restricting raw material supply, not by demand growth; tariff landscape remains a swing factor

items.target: Sustained market strength expected to continue into FY26
items.notes: Supported by Northern Hemisphere pollock price strength; downside risk flagged from trade-policy disruption

items.target: Prices expected to remain steady; demand still moderated
items.notes: Reflects a subdued Chinese economy weighing on discretionary high-value seafood demand

items.target: Continued disciplined/low capex; ~$6.7m in HY26 (annualising well below FY25's $23.3m)
items.notes: Management explicitly favouring further debt reduction and balance-sheet strength over growth capex until the strategic review concludes, to be 'in a good position to take advantage of investment opportunities as and when they arise'

items.target: Continued reduction from $102.1m net debt at HY26
items.notes: MD: 'My intention is to reduce debt further, positioning the company on a more solid platform'

items.target: 5.0 cps interim (HY26), consistent with 5.0 cps interim/final through FY25
items.notes: Board explicitly prioritising balance-sheet strengthening over faster dividend growth: 'A conservative dividend profile ... assists share performance by strengthening the company's balance sheet'

items.target: Initial high-level review of aquaculture (salmon and mussels) assets completed in HY26; wildcatch review (fishing-partner, inshore ACE, scampi and fillet-vessel assets) still ongoing
items.notes: MD reported the aquaculture asset review found low-capital, low-risk mussel growth opportunities (new vessel, Western Firth of Thames consent) but the wildcatch review remains unresolved; outcome could include further asset sales, capacity reallocation or exit from sub-scale species

guidance.management_commentary: Chair and MD both frame FY25/HY26 as validating the 'Back to Basics' program of cost discipline, SKU rationalisation and balance-sheet repair rather than top-line growth (revenue was flat-to-down in both periods while margins and profit hit records). Management is explicit that Big Glory Bay salmon has no near-term growth runway, that wildcatch is 'operating as a commodity player' with limited growth optionality under the QMS, and that mussels is the low-risk/low-capital growth avenue being actively invested in (Western Firth of Thames consent, new vessel, SPATnz hatchery scale-up, unused existing water space). The strategic review of aquaculture fixed assets is now largely complete and directionally low-risk/mussel-led; the wildcatch review remains unresolved and is the primary swing factor for medium-term capital allocation and portfolio shape. Analyst consensus (thin coverage, effectively one or two brokers) currently rates the stock a Hold/Neutral with price targets in the roughly NZ$7.30-9.50 range, broadly above the prevailing NZ$7.00-7.30 share price.

bull_case: Deep value re-rate still in progress: at ~NZ$7.00-7.30/share and ~93.6m shares (~NZ$650-680m market cap), the stock trades close to or below FY25 net asset backing per share (~$7.92) and around 9-10x trailing NPAT, despite delivering three consecutive record profit halves/years and a dramatically repaired balance sheet (net debt cut from $185.5m to $93.4m to $102.1m across FY24/FY25/HY26)

Margin expansion looks structural, not purely cyclical: SKU rationalisation, a push-to-pull operating model, and organisational simplification are all process changes management explicitly frames as producing 'sustainable business improvements' rather than one-off gains, and gross margin has now expanded in three straight halves (21.6% to 26.5% to 28.2% to 33.7%)

Low-risk, high-return mussel growth pipeline (Western Firth of Thames consent, record SPATnz hatchery output, new efficient vessel, 20-year permit extension to 2044, unused existing water space) offers a credible volume-growth vector that does not require the company to take on Big Glory Bay-style biological/environmental risk

Quota and consented water space are a durable, hard-to-replicate asset base (~$486m of intangibles, ~19.8% of national QMS quota) underpinning the business against new entrants and carried at historic cost well below likely market value, understating true book value; Sanford's own Big Glory Bay salmon site has so far avoided the catastrophic warm-water mortality events that have hit Marlborough Sounds competitors

Disciplined capital allocation under new leadership (record-low capex of $23.3m in FY25 and $6.7m in HY26) is prioritising debt paydown, creating dry powder for value-accretive investment once the wildcatch strategic review concludes, with a strengthened board (Tony Carter's food/distribution experience) supporting execution
bear_case: FY25/HY26 earnings quality is questionable: a meaningful share of the profit beat is non-operating (a $17.5m favourable salmon biological-asset fair-value gain in HY26 alone versus $3.3m a year earlier), and gross margin gains partly reflect a temporary, unusually favourable mussel harvest yield in the South Island that management itself says will not repeat at the same level in FY26 — this is a business whose recent 'record' results were flattered by weather/biology, not solely demonstrated pricing power, and HY26 operating cash flow fell sharply (to $13.7m from $49.6m) on rising frozen inventory

Revenue has been flat-to-declining even through the 'record' periods (FY25 revenue +0.2%, HY26 revenue -5.5%), meaning the profit growth story rests heavily on margin/cost actions with a shrinking runway once the low-hanging SKU/cost fruit is picked, while two of three pillars (Wildcatch, and now salmon at its Big Glory Bay ceiling) have explicit no-growth outlooks from management

The core moat asset (fishing quota, roughly half of total assets) is directly exposed to regulator discretion on TACC-setting — the FY25/26 orange roughy cuts and proposed spawning-area closures on the Chatham Rise already constrain Timaru volumes, and the pending Fisheries Amendment Bill 2026 changes how catch limits and deemed-value rates are set, introducing structural uncertainty (and litigation risk, per the March 2025 High Court ruling against a prior ministerial quota decision) to a large intangible asset that cannot be diversified away

Big Glory Bay's cold-water advantage over Marlborough Sounds mitigates but does not eliminate the sector's demonstrated vulnerability to marine heatwaves, and the site's hard nitrogen cap means Sanford has no near-term ability to relocate or expand salmon capacity even if conditions there also deteriorated — the highest-margin segment has a structural growth ceiling and an unhedged tail climate risk simultaneously

The ~9.6% Ngai Tahu block-trade sell-down in June 2026 (raising ~$64m, halving its stake to ~19.9%) signals a large, informed cornerstone holder was willing to materially cut its position after the 'Back to Basics' run-up, and thin analyst coverage plus a Hold/Neutral consensus rating suggest the market is not yet convinced the re-rating story has further to run before the unresolved wildcatch strategic review produces a concrete outcome
